title: Adenoidectomy
subtitle: Feel the palate first, spare the tori and the lower fringe

sources.org: American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery Foundation (AAO-HNSF)
sources.title: Clinical Practice Guideline: Tympanostomy Tubes in Children (Update)

sources.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
sources.title: Otitis media with effusion in under 12s (NG233)

sources.org: American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery Foundation (AAO-HNSF)
sources.title: Clinical Practice Guideline: Tonsillectomy in Children (Update)

indications: Nasal obstruction with mouth breathing, snoring or obstructive sleep-disordered breathing from adenoid hypertrophy, alone or with tonsillectomy.

As an adjunct to grommet insertion in selected children with otitis media with effusion. It is not a routine addition: the AAO-HNSF tympanostomy tube guideline advises against it in young children without a separate indication, and NICE NG233 sets out when it is considered.
Chronic adenoiditis or chronic rhinosinusitis in a child after failed medical treatment.
Suspicion of nasopharyngeal pathology in an adult: this is a biopsy, not an adenoidectomy, and needs imaging and a different plan.
contraindications: Cleft palate, submucous cleft or known velopharyngeal insufficiency. A partial (superior) adenoidectomy may be considered after specialist discussion; a full adenoidectomy risks hypernasal speech.
Uncorrected bleeding disorder. Take a bleeding history from the parents in every child.
Atlantoaxial instability, for example in some children with Down syndrome, unless neck positioning has been planned with the anaesthetist.
Active upper respiratory tract infection at the time of an elective list, which raises both anaesthetic and bleeding risk.
preparation: Confirm the indication in the record: obstructive symptoms or a sleep study, or the audiogram and tympanogram if done with grommets.
Ask specifically about nasal regurgitation of feeds and hypernasal speech, which suggest velopharyngeal problems, and about loose teeth.
Plan the setting: children under 3 and those with severe obstructive sleep apnoea or significant comorbidity may need overnight monitoring, as for adenotonsillectomy.

Consent risks to discuss: bleeding, including the rare need to return to theatre or for a postnasal pack, damage to teeth, lips and gums, temporary voice change and nasal regurgitation, persistent hypernasal speech, regrowth of adenoid tissue, neck stiffness and rarely atlantoaxial subluxation (Grisel syndrome), and nasopharyngeal scarring.
positioning: Supine on a head ring with a shoulder roll and moderate neck extension, so the nasopharynx is visible behind the soft palate.
Mouth gag with a tongue blade sized for the child, the tube sitting in the groove, suspended on Draffin rods or a holder.
Moderate extension in any child with suspected atlantoaxial instability.
equipment: Boyle-Davis or equivalent gag, a range of tongue blades and a preformed oral tube.
Laryngeal mirror and headlight, or a 0 or 70 degree endoscope through the mouth or nose, to see the nasopharynx.
Soft rubber catheter passed through the nose and out of the mouth to retract the soft palate.
Suction diathermy, coblation wand, or adenoid curettes of several sizes, according to the technique chosen. Postnasal pack and tonsil swabs, counted.
anatomy: The adenoid is lymphoid tissue on the roof and posterior wall of the nasopharynx, above the free edge of the soft palate.
The torus tubarius and Eustachian tube openings are on the lateral walls. Injury causes scarring and tubal dysfunction.
Behind the posterior wall lie the prevertebral fascia, the longus colli and capitis and the atlas and axis. Deep curettage or diathermy here can cause neck pain and, rarely, atlantoaxial subluxation.
The inferior part of the adenoid pad helps the soft palate close the nasopharynx during speech. Removing the lower fringe in a child with a short or weak palate can cause hypernasal speech.
The blood supply comes from branches of the ascending pharyngeal, ascending palatine and pharyngeal branch of the maxillary artery. Bleeding is usually from residual tags.
criticalSafety: Palpate the soft palate before removing any adenoid. A notch in the hard palate, a bifid uvula or a translucent midline zone suggests a submucous cleft.
Work under vision with a mirror or endoscope. Blind curettage misses lateral tissue and injures the tori.
Stay superficial on the posterior wall. Do not dig into the prevertebral tissue.
Clear the nasopharynx of clot and remove the postnasal pack before the gag comes out.
structuresAtRisk: Torus tubarius and Eustachian tube orifices
Teeth, lips and gums under the gag
commonErrors: Skipping palatal palpation and missing a submucous cleft.
Leaving adenoid tissue in the choanae or around the tori, so the obstruction persists.
Using a curette too large for the nasopharynx, which reaches the tori and the prevertebral tissue.
Declaring haemostasis with the gag still open and the pack just removed.
complications: Primary haemorrhage, which may need a postnasal pack under anaesthesia, and less often secondary haemorrhage.
Velopharyngeal insufficiency with hypernasal speech and nasal regurgitation, usually temporary and occasionally persistent.
Neck pain and stiffness; rarely Grisel syndrome (non-traumatic atlantoaxial subluxation), which presents with torticollis days after surgery and needs urgent assessment.
Dental injury, regrowth of adenoid tissue, nasopharyngeal stenosis and Eustachian tube dysfunction.
postop: Recover in the lateral position with head slightly down. Bleeding from the nose or mouth, or repeated swallowing, needs immediate review.
Regular paracetamol and ibuprofen are usually enough. Do not give codeine to children under 12.
Warn parents about snoring and nasal discharge for a week or two, and to return if the child bleeds, develops a stiff or twisted neck, or has nasal regurgitation that does not settle.

steps.emphasis: Ask the parents about bleeding in the family, nasal regurgitation of feeds and loose teeth.
Obstructive symptoms or sleep study, or audiogram and tympanogram if grommets are planned. Confirm whether tonsillectomy is also consented.
No routine antibiotic prophylaxis. Dexamethasone if combined with tonsillectomy, per the anaesthetic plan.
Preformed oral tube. Agree that the anaesthetist will watch ventilation pressures as the gag opens.
Moderate extension only, and less in any child with possible atlantoaxial instability.
Look for loose deciduous teeth before the gag goes in; a loose tooth is removed deliberately and accounted for, not lost.
Remove the pack, release the gag for a minute, re-open and look at the nasopharynx again with the mirror or endoscope.
Postnasal pack and every tonsil swab counted out before the gag is removed.
Adenoid tissue is not always sent. Send it if the appearance is unusual, the patient is an adult, or local policy requires it.
Lateral position. Fresh blood from the nose or mouth, or repeated swallowing, means bleeding until examined.

step.adeno.gag-palate.title: Insert the gag and palpate the palate
step.adeno.gag-palate.why: A submucous cleft is easy to miss by looking and easy to find by feeling. Removing the adenoid in a child with a cleft can leave them with permanent hypernasal speech.
how: Open and suspend the gag, checking the tube, teeth and lips as it opens.
Inspect the uvula for a bifid tip and the soft palate for a translucent midline zone.
Run a finger along the hard palate to its posterior edge, feeling for a notch where the posterior nasal spine should be.
If a submucous cleft is suspected, stop. Do not remove the adenoid; discuss a partial adenoidectomy or referral to the cleft team.
pitfalls: Palpating after the adenoid has been removed, when the information is no longer useful.
Proceeding with a full adenoidectomy despite a bifid uvula because the list is running late.

step.adeno.view.title: See the nasopharynx
step.adeno.view.why: Adenoid tissue in the choanae and around the tori is what causes persisting obstruction and ear disease, and it cannot be judged by feel. Seeing it also shows where the tori are before anything is removed.
how: Pass a soft catheter through one or both nostrils, out of the mouth, and clip it to retract the soft palate forwards.
View the nasopharynx with a warmed laryngeal mirror and headlight, or an endoscope, and note the size of the adenoid, its relation to the choanae and the position of both tori.
Look for anything that is not adenoid: an unusual mass, a lesion in an adult, or an aberrant pulsation.
pitfalls: Tensioning the palatal catheter so hard that it blanches or tears the palate.
Assuming the nasopharynx is normal because it was normal on palpation.

step.adeno.removal.title: Remove the adenoid under vision, superficially
step.adeno.removal.why: The aim is a clear airway and choanae with the tori, the prevertebral tissue and the velopharyngeal fringe intact. Each technique can achieve that if it is used under vision and kept superficial.
how: With suction diathermy or coblation, start at the choanae and work backwards and downwards across the pad under mirror or endoscopic vision, ablating the tissue rather than burning the posterior wall.

With a curette, choose a size that fits between the tori, place it against the posterior border of the septum, and sweep down the posterior wall in one firm movement, keeping the handle against the upper teeth only as a guide, not a lever.
Clear tissue around the choanae and the tori carefully, without touching the tori themselves.
In a child at risk of velopharyngeal insufficiency, leave the inferior fringe where the palate meets the posterior wall.
pitfalls: Diathermy held on the posterior wall until it chars, which damages the prevertebral tissue and adds to neck pain.
A curette sweep that goes too deep and too low, removing the fringe and scraping prevertebral fascia.

step.adeno.pack.title: Postnasal pack and wait
step.adeno.pack.why: After curettage most bleeding is from raw lymphoid tissue and stops with pressure. A timed pack also lets small residual tags declare themselves.
how: Place a counted postnasal pack, with a tie or string left outside the mouth, into the nasopharynx after curettage. Record its placement.
Leave it for a few minutes, or do the tonsils or ears meanwhile if planned.
Remove it and inspect again, removing residual tags with forceps or treating them with suction diathermy.
pitfalls: A pack without a tie, which can be pushed up into the nasopharynx and forgotten.
A pack placed and not recorded on the whiteboard.

step.adeno.bleed-bailout.title: Bail-out: bleeding that will not stop
step.adeno.bleed-bailout.why: Persistent nasopharyngeal bleeding in a small child becomes a volume problem quickly, and the blood loss is hidden because it is swallowed. A deliberate escalation avoids an unplanned return to theatre at night.
how: Look for residual tissue, especially in the choanae and lateral recesses, and remove or treat it.
Use suction diathermy on discrete bleeding points under vision, avoiding the tori.

If bleeding persists, place a postnasal pack secured with ties brought out through the nose, keep the child intubated or monitored according to the anaesthetist's plan, and arrange high-dependency care.
Tell the consultant, estimate blood loss against the child's blood volume, send a full blood count and coagulation screen, and look for an undiagnosed bleeding disorder.
pitfalls: Repeated curettage of a bleeding nasopharynx, which makes it worse.
Underestimating blood loss in a small child because it was swallowed rather than suctioned.
